quotes.text: He was a naturally gifted songwriter, had a great voice, and had exceptional timing – John Denver couldn't have been the phenomenon that he was in 1975 had he come along instead in 1965 or 1985, few people meshed with the zeitgeist in the early 70s like Denver.

He was a sensitive singer-songwriter in The Golden Age of the Sensitive Singer-Songwriter, he oozed wholesomeness at a time when a significant part of the American population was pulling back from the excesses of the 60s, and the dude could write a catchy tune about mountains and sunshine and country roads at a time when more people began thinking a lot about getting back to the great outdoors.

Being himself was a long-term problem, because when the zeitgeist no longer favored guys like him, he couldn't pull a David Bowie or a Madonna and morph to fit the times. He was stuck still being himself once music trends had left guys like him far behind.
Denver wrote mostly in the folk-country music genres, although he had some crossover success with Annie's Song, which he wrote for his first wife, Annie Martell-Denver.
quotes.publication: Music Album Review: The Essential John Denver

quotes.text: He co-wrote (with Fat City's Bill Danoff and Taffy Nivert) Take Me Home, Country Roads, and (with Dick Kniss and Mike Taylor) the top-charting song for 1973, Sunshine on My Shoulders.

quotes.text: John Denver's music represents the very best in art... he's a very good folk singer who picks up themes that are universal and positive and life-enhancing.
So it's semi-Tchaikovsky, mostly-Denver. It was John's idea to do a whole chorus of humming.

The songs in this album are melodic, wonderfully crafted, and have become part of the American musical canon. So much so, in fact, that many professionals singers and producers put him on the pantheon of great American songwriters, in the company of Stephen Foster, Irving Berlin, Jerome Kern, and George and Ira Gershwin.

John Denver's whole persona, which was probably pretty close to his actual self, was always "sentimental outdoorsy guy." He couldn't even write a simple love song to his wife without comparing her to mountains and lakes and shit. You have to respect the man's focus.
This was how Denver knew to communicate. And because there's something so inherently romantic about all this imagery, those bone-simple similes work.
"Annie's Song" is a piece of work so sincerely sentimental that it risks absolute corniness. But that sincerity is why it works.

Over an ornate, delicate acoustic-guitar figure, Denver wholeheartedly intones all that stuff about mountains and oceans, and then, in terms so heart-shatteringly vulnerable that they're almost embarrassing to hear, he asks her to spend her life with him.
The melody is elementally simple, almost hymnlike. Even before they show up, though the song sounds grand and epic. It's syrup, but it's good syrup.
And yet "Annie's Song" still stands as a feeling trapped in amber -- a man trying to explain his total (if not eternal) devotion in the only way he knows.
